items.basis: Spacer-induced shear stress enhancement fails to address the fundamental chemistry of SMP/EPS adhesion, which is primarily driven by electrostatic interactions and hydrophobic bonding, not removable by shear forces alone as demonstrated in the evidence regarding zinc oxide nanoparticles' effects on SMP composition (doi:10.1007/s11356-026-38139-3).

The candidate fails to specify critical boundary conditions including flow rates, spacer geometry specifications, membrane packing density, and wastewater characteristics, making the proposed solution unverifiable and potentially ineffective under real-world municipal wastewater conditions with variable organic loads and seasonal temperature fluctuations.

The evidence provided shows conflicting results, with some studies showing fouling reduction through air sparging (doi:10.1016/j.desal.2009.09.140) while others demonstrate persistent fouling issues despite similar interventions, indicating the proposed spacer mechanism may not consistently outperform existing methods.

The candidate provides no comparative data demonstrating that spacer-equipped modules outperform conventional systems in long-term operation, and the referenced studies on hollow-fiber modules (doi:10.30684/etj.30.19.14) show no significant improvement in permeability maintenance over the standard baseline.

Integrating spacer elements between membrane fibers would require complete re-engineering of existing hollow-fiber module manufacturing processes, increasing capital costs by an estimated 40-60% without corresponding evidence of sufficient operational benefits to justify the expense.

The testable prediction of measuring transmembrane pressure increase rate fails to account for confounding variables such as biofilm development, seasonal variations in wastewater composition, and differences in aeration patterns that would independently affect pressure readings, rendering the proposed measurement methodology inadequate for isolating the spacer effect.
